label: Get the Job — Positioning
overview: The Get the Job — Positioning content teaches advisors how to move from being a transactional 'vendor of hours' to a trusted authority. It covers four core frameworks: how to categorise and structure client engagements (Three Engagement Types), how to assess growth constraints in any business (CCO), how to dismantle the once-a-year meeting mentality (Helicopter Story), and how to achieve total personal congruence in client interactions (Mastering Positioning). Intermediate-level content suited to senior advisors focused on fee growth.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: What is the primary challenge you are working on — understanding how to structure an engagement, assessing a client's growth potential, convincing a client to meet more regularly, or building your own personal authority and trust in client relationships?

support_tools.name: Three Engagement Types
support_tools.purpose: A framework for categorising every client interaction as Advice, Facilitation, or Education — and defining the advisor's correct role, delivery position, and imperative for each type.
support_tools.core_principle: Engagements must be driven by what the client genuinely needs, not by what the advisor wants to sell. The 'Look Both Ways' approach — examining pre-event causes and post-event effects — naturally extends the engagement arena without the client ever feeling up-sold.
support_tools.when_to_use: Whenever the advisor needs to define the nature of the work before beginning. Particularly useful when a client presents a specific trigger event (e.g., a loan drawdown, a business purchase, a compliance issue) — the advisor categorises the work before proposing a scope.
key_benefits: Prevents misaligned engagements — the advisor knows their position (hierarchical for advice, professionally detached for facilitation) before the meeting begins
The 'Look Both Ways' method surfaces pre-event work (feasibility) and post-event work (management meetings) that the client often hasn't considered
Removes the pressure to up-sell — additional work arises naturally from examining cause and effect
Gives the client clear expectations: they know whether they are receiving advice, being facilitated through a process, or being educated
support_tools.advisor_confidence_note: Identify the driver first — consequence, trigger event, or knowledge gap — before selecting the engagement type. If the client is facing a loan drawdown, the pre-event work (feasibility) and post-event work (management meetings post-drawdown) are both legitimate engagement opportunities that you can raise without it feeling like a pitch.

steps.name: Identify the driver
steps.guidance: Determine if the client is facing a clear consequence (requiring direct advice), a trigger event (requiring facilitation), or a knowledge gap (requiring education). This determines everything that follows.

steps.name: Determine the engagement type
steps.guidance: Categorise the work as Advice (hierarchical position, accuracy imperative), Facilitation (professionally detached, reveal imperative), or Education (sequential comprehension, chunking imperative).

steps.name: Look both ways
steps.guidance: Examine the cause/pre-event (e.g., feasibility of a loan) and the effect/post-event (e.g., management meetings after drawdown). Both may represent legitimate paid work the client hasn't yet considered.

steps.name: Deliver on the imperative
steps.guidance: For Advice: prioritise accuracy. For Facilitation: build to the reveal moment. For Education: chunk the content into sequential, digestible steps — never overwhelm.

support_tools.name: Capacity, Capability, Opportunity (CCO)
support_tools.purpose: A structured diagnostic framework for evaluating how a business can realistically grow — separating physical constraints (Capacity), skill and financial limitations (Capability), and market realities (Opportunity).
support_tools.core_principle: Growth conversations become unfocused when all three dimensions are conflated. CCO separates them deliberately — a business may have the opportunity and capability to grow but lack the physical capacity, or have capacity and opportunity but not the financial resources to fund the next step.
support_tools.when_to_use: When advising a business aiming to scale, increase transaction volumes, or move into new premium markets. Can be used internally as a diagnostic before the client meeting, or presented externally as the meeting agenda itself.
key_benefits: Provides a structured, three-part diagnostic that the advisor can use internally to find areas to add value — without solving everything on the spot
Acts as a perfect entry point to introduce additional services naturally, without it feeling like up-selling
Clearly separates physical bottlenecks (capacity) from skill/financial gaps (capability) from market demand issues (opportunity)
Can be used as a formal agenda structure: each dimension becomes an agenda item with its own discussion
support_tools.advisor_confidence_note: CCO does not need to be formally presented every time. Use it internally first to identify where the value gaps are, then raise the most relevant dimension with the client. The goal is to find the one constraint that, if removed, would have the greatest impact — not to solve all three at once.

steps.name: Assess Capacity
steps.guidance: Evaluate whether the business can physically produce more or handle higher transactional volume — check downtime, machinery limits, team availability, and whether bottlenecks exist.

steps.name: Assess Capability
steps.guidance: Evaluate whether the business has the skills, personnel depth, and financial resources to support the growth. Look at staff expertise, management depth, and funding access.

steps.name: Assess Opportunity
steps.guidance: Look for proof of strong market demand from existing or new clients before proceeding. If demand is not there, growing capacity or capability will not solve the problem.

steps.name: Frame the discussion
steps.guidance: Introduce CCO formally as the agenda structure for the meeting, or use it silently as your internal diagnostic — then surface only the most critical finding with the client.

support_tools.name: Helicopter Story
support_tools.purpose: A visual whiteboard analogy that challenges the flawed logic of once-a-year accounting meetings by showing the client how dangerous it is to navigate a volatile business environment without a regular 'flight plan' review.
support_tools.core_principle: The advisor is the Air Control Tower. A pilot who only calls the tower once a year is flying blind. Once the client accepts this analogy, asking for regular strategic meetings becomes the logical conclusion — not a sales pitch.
support_tools.when_to_use: When a client resists regular advisory check-ins or views accounting as an annual compliance exercise. Use in a first or second meeting to reframe the relationship before proposing a recurring advisory schedule.
key_benefits: Dismantles the 'once a year' mentality using a visual analogy — no data or spreadsheets required
Positions the advisor as an essential Air Control Tower rather than a reactive compliance service
The 'blindfold' metaphor makes the risk of poor internal reporting immediately tangible to the client
The 'three-ton load' (representing internal fraud or high-impact events) creates urgency without scaremongering
support_tools.advisor_confidence_note: Draw the story as you tell it — this is a whiteboard or paper exercise, not a slide deck. Start with the wavy ground (seasonal volatility) and mountain (high-impact events). Build to the blindfolded pilot. Ask: 'What use is the Air Control Tower if the pilot only calls once a year?' Then hand the question back: 'How often do you feel you should meet to review your strategic flight plan?'

steps.name: Draw the scene
steps.guidance: Illustrate wavy ground (high frequency, low impact seasonal volatility) and a mountain (high impact events like market crashes or fraud).

steps.name: Introduce the helicopter
steps.guidance: The helicopter is the business. The pilot is the business owner. The dashboard is their internal reporting.

steps.name: Apply the blindfold
steps.guidance: Show how inaccurate or untimely financial data puts a blindfold on the pilot — they are flying the business without being able to see the terrain.

phases.name: Position the Tower and Secure the Meeting

steps.name: Draw the control tower
steps.guidance: Draw the control tower (the advisor) and ask: 'What use is the control tower if the pilot only calls once a year?'

steps.name: Secure the meeting commitment
steps.guidance: Hand the question back to the client: 'How often do you feel you should meet to discuss your strategic flight plan?' Let them arrive at the answer.

support_tools.name: Mastering Positioning
support_tools.purpose: A behavioural guide for shifting from selling a service (what you do) to selling yourself (who you are) — achieving total congruence between technical advice, body language, tone of voice, and fundamental values to build biological trust.
support_tools.core_principle: Trust is biological. If your tone or body language triggers a client's chemical survival response (norepinephrine), the logic of your advice will not matter. Positioning is about occupying a space of trust and authority before any spreadsheet is opened.
support_tools.when_to_use: In all prospect and client interactions — particularly initial meetings where trust and authority are still being established. This is not a technique to deploy situationally; it is a permanent shift in how the advisor shows up.
key_benefits: Removes friction from the advisory process — when the client is relaxed and trusting, influence is far easier
Shifts the competitive battleground from service comparison (commoditised) to personal identity (unique)
Total congruence — matching technical advice with body language, tone, and values — prevents the biological trust breakdown that derails good advice
Establishes the 'somatic connection': the unspoken feeling of alignment that opens the door to collaborative influence
support_tools.advisor_confidence_note: A sales pitch focuses on what you do. Positioning is about who you are. Before any meeting, set your strategic intent: 'I am here to occupy a space of trust and authority.' Monitor the vibe in the room — a poor vibe signals the client's survival response has been triggered. Slow down, align your tone and body language, and let the somatic connection re-establish before proceeding.

steps.name: Focus on the client's mind
steps.guidance: Before opening a spreadsheet, set your strategic intent to occupy a space of trust and authority. This is the foundation from which all other positioning flows.

steps.name: Align your delivery (congruence)
steps.guidance: Ensure your technical advice perfectly matches your body language, tone of voice, and fundamental values. Incongruence between these triggers scepticism regardless of how good the advice is.

steps.name: Monitor the vibe
steps.guidance: Be aware that a poor vibe can trigger the client's chemical survival response (norepinephrine), making them defensive and risk-averse. If the room feels off, do not push harder — slow down and re-align.

steps.name: Establish the somatic connection
steps.guidance: Aim for the unspoken feeling of alignment — the point where the client relaxes and true collaborative influence becomes possible. This is the moment positioning has worked.

advisor_guidance.sequence: These four frameworks work together in sequence. CCO diagnoses the growth constraints. Three Engagement Types structures how you will address them. Helicopter Story secures the regular meeting cadence. Mastering Positioning ensures your delivery lands as intended.
advisor_guidance.internal_vs_external: CCO and Three Engagement Types can both be used as internal diagnostic tools before the meeting — the client never needs to see the framework. Only surface what is most useful to them in the room.
advisor_guidance.positioning_is_permanent: Positioning is not a technique you deploy in the first meeting and then abandon. It is a permanent operating mode. Advisors who revert to transactional behaviour after the first meeting undo the trust they built.
